title: It is I, fear not (Mark 6:45–56)
hookLine: he walks on the sea and sees them toiling in rowing

cards: Three in the morning. You're pulling at something that won't move: a deadline, a sick child's fever, a relationship drifting backward however hard you work. Your arms ache, and you're pretty sure no one sees.
That's where the disciples are tonight. Right after the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus sends them across the lake by boat while he stays behind to pray. The wind turns against them.
They row for hours and get nowhere.

teach.b: First, he sees. He has gone up the mountain to pray; the boat is in the middle of the sea, and he is alone on the land. In the Douay-Rheims he is "seeing them labouring in rowing", with the wind against them.
They think they're alone out there. They aren't. Second, he comes.
In the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, he comes to them walking on the sea.
Then Mark adds a strange line: he would have passed by them.
Some readers hear an echo of the Hebrew Bible, where God passes by Moses on the mountain, and Elijah at the cave; in those stories, passing by is how God shows himself. Third, the word.
The disciples think he's a ghost, and scream. Straightaway he speaks: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not."

teach.h: EGO EIMI: IT IS I, I AM.
teach.b: In Mark's Greek, it is I is ego eimi, which some readers also hear as I am, the name God gives Moses at the burning bush; the Douay-Rheims has it as I am who am.
Heard that way, the words carry two things at once: it's me, your friend, don't be afraid; and, I am. Fourth, the boat.

teach.h: THE WIND DROPS; THEY STILL DON'T SEE.
teach.b: He climbs in, and the wind drops. They were astonished, Mark says, because they hadn't understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened.

teach.h: HAVE A GOOD HEART, IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.
teach.b: Mark's disciples still don't get it. Then they land, and people rush the sick to him on mats, begging just to touch the hem of his garment, and all who touch it are healed.
Peter's walk on the water is in Matthew's telling, not Mark's. Mark keeps his eyes on the rowers.

how: Mark's account of the walking on the water is read at a weekday Mass in the Christmas season, after Epiphany, and Pope John Paul II opened his papacy with the words 'be not afraid'.

o: a promise that the storm will soon end
it's me, and also the name God gave Moses
a ghost's cry from out on the dark water

games.q: it's the fourth watch. you've rowed all night against the wind. a figure is walking toward you on the water, and you think it's a ghost. what does he say?
o: why did you leave without me?
have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not.
games.why: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not." then he gets into the boat, and the wind drops.

practice: Picture a small boat at night, put yourself at the oars, and name plainly what you're pulling against right now: a task, a person, an illness, a fear.
If you pray, hear the words spoken into that boat: have a good heart, it is I, fear not. If you don't, let your tired arms rest, and let the wind blow.

wordCard.voice: I am. Jesus's words on the water: ego eimi, it's me, and I am, the name God gave Moses. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: it is I, or I am; the same words can echo God's name to Moses.

carryVoice: Your line: have a good heart. The rowers weren't as alone as they thought. Two hundred nine days now.

sources.q: Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not.
